newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - French rate cut spotlights new cen bankers.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - French rate cut spotlights new cen bankers.

text.p: The Bank of France surprised financial markets by trimming a key interest rate on Thursday, reviving speculation that the appointment of two "doves" to its policy-setting council may have changed the balance of power within the bank.

The central bank eased its intervention rate to 3.10 percent from 3.15 after a meeting of its monetary policy council, surprising most economists who said earlier this week that the recent rise in the dollar had lowered the chances of a rate cut.
"I didn't think they'd do it this week," said Jean-Louis Mourier, economist at Louis Dreyfus Finance. "The market was not convinced either."

The move revived talk in Paris that the appointment this month of Pierre Guillen and Jean-Rene Bernard to the nine-member council has changed the Bank's traditionally cautious policy stance and could lead to faster interest rate cuts.

Both men are seen as close to President Jacques Chirac and reported to favour easier monetary policy. They replaced two men considered staunch supporters of the Bank's hawkish governor, Jean-Claude Trichet.
Some economists said Thursday's cut looked like the first evidence of the new members' influence.

"I believe Trichet would have wanted to wait for the (U.S. Federal Reserve Federal Open Market Committee) FOMC decision next week," said Eric Chaney, economist at Morgan Stanley in Paris. "But the doves wanted to send a strong message, so this might be a compromise."
"It might be a move intended to show there is room to cut independently of the Fed and the Bundesbank," Chaney said.
The FOMC meets next week and will consider whether to raise its federal funds rate amid signs the U.S. economy is buoyant.
Many economists had expected the Bank of France to take advantage of the expansionary effect of a rising dollar and wait to cut rates and thus were doubly-surprised by the decision.
"It seems the doves are decisive, it's not just a dream... They'll cut further in the coming months," said ABN Amro economist Philippe Brossard.
"It caught the market off guard...in terms of the timing, but not at all in terms of the fact of it," added Sonja Gibbs, a bond analyst with Nomura International in London.
Most private economists have expected for some time that the independent central bank would gradually bring the intervention rate down to the three-percent level of the German repo rate.
The Bank has traditionally maintained a small premium over the repo rate to cushion the franc against speculative attack.
But markets expect the German and French interest rates to converge before currency parities are locked in preparation for European monetary union, due in January 1999.
"This is no longer for the sake of the economy, it's all about convergence for EMU, for afterwards," Mourier said.

One economist dismissed talk about the role of the council's new members as "futile" and said the rate cut was simply a continuation of the Bank's tested policy of cautiously lowering rates to boost French confidence and growth prospects.
"It was expected and is in line with the idea of a cautious trend toward the floor level of German rates," said Herve Goulletquer, economist with Banques Populaires.
Industrialists and the centre-right government have been pressing for lower interest rates to boost a sluggish economy and bring down record 12.7 percent unemployment.
The franc barely blinked after the rate cut, trading nearly unchanged at 3.3750 to the mark at 1600 GMT.
The intervention rate was last cut from 3.20 percent, on December 17. The Bank left its five-to-10 day emergency lending rate, considered less important now, unchanged at 4.60 percent.
